lines.text: How can an atom occupy far more space than its nucleus?
An atom is mostly empty space. Its very small, dense nucleus contains protons and neutrons, electrons occupy shells around it.

Use this idea with the particle counts, charge and shell comparisons in this chapter. Next, the charges and masses of these particles, one point one point two, show why the nucleus carries the mass, shells return in Electrons, energy levels and atomic orbitals.
Nucleus, small and dense, with protons and neutrons. Electrons occupy surrounding shells in mostly empty space.
How can an atom be mostly empty space yet contain a dense nucleus?

Where are an atom's electrons? In the nucleus In shells around the nucleus Between protons and neutrons Uniformly throughout a solid atom B Electrons occupy shells around the tiny nucleus, most of the atom is empty space.
Particle masses explain where almost all atomic mass lies.
A proton has relative charge plus one and mass one, a neutron has charge zero and mass one, an electron has charge minus one and mass about one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six.

Use this idea with the particle counts, charge and shell comparisons in this chapter. Next, count these particles from Z and ay, one point one point three, the tiny electron mass explains why electron beams bend most, one point one point five.
Proton, charge plus one, mass one, neutron, charge zero, mass one. Electron, charge minus one, mass about one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six.
Why does removing an electron barely change atomic mass?

Which relative charge and mass belong to an electron? plus one and one zero and one minus one and one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six minus one and one C An electron has charge minus one and relative mass about one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six.
Two numbers beside an element symbol identify its protons and nucleons.
Proton number, atomic number, Z is the number of protons in the nucleus. Nucleon number, mass number, ay is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Neutrons equals ay minus Z.

Use this idea with the particle counts, charge and shell comparisons in this chapter. Next, an ion changes only the electron count, one point one point six, atoms with the same Z but different A are the isotopes of Isotopes.
Proton number Z counts protons and defines the element. Nucleon number A counts protons plus neutrons.
Why can atoms of the same element have different nucleon numbers?

A nucleus has thirteen protons and fourteen neutrons. What are Z and ay? Z equals thirteen, ay equals twenty seven Z equals fourteen, ay equals twenty seven Z equals thirteen, ay equals fourteen Z equals twenty seven, ay equals thirteen ay The proton number is thirteen, the nucleon number is thirteen plus fourteen equals twenty seven.
The charges of a neutral atom occupy different regions.
Nearly all atomic mass and all positive charge lie in the nucleus. Negative charge lies in the electron shells. Equal proton and electron counts make a neutral atom overall.

Use this idea with the particle counts, charge and shell comparisons in this chapter. Next, where the charges sit decides how beams bend in an electric field, one point one point five, and how an ion gets its charge, one point one point six.
Nucleus, nearly all mass and all positive charge. Shells, negative electron charge, equal proton and electron counts give neutrality.
How can the whole atom be neutral when its nucleus is positive?

Where are nearly all the mass and all the positive charge? The nucleus The electron shells Evenly throughout the atom The empty space between shells ay Protons and neutrons give the nucleus nearly all the mass, protons give it positive charge.
Beams in an electric field reveal particle charge and mass.

At equal velocity, protons bend towards the negative plate, electrons towards the positive plate, and neutrons remain undeflected. Electrons bend more than protons because their charge to mass ratio is much larger.

Use this idea with the particle counts, charge and shell comparisons in this chapter. Same force, smaller mass, larger acceleration, the charge and mass values of one point one point two at work. Next, ion charges come from protons minus electrons, one point one point six.
Protons bend towards the negative plate, electrons towards the positive plate. Neutrons do not bend, electrons bend more than protons.
Why do proton and electron beams bend in opposite directions?
Which beam is undeflected by an electric field? Protons Neutrons Electrons All three B Neutrons have zero charge, so the electric field does not deflect them.
An ion's charge changes its electron count but not its nuclear counts.

Protons equals Z and neutrons equals ay minus Z. A neutral atom has Z electrons. For an ion, electrons equals Z minus signed charge, subtract a positive charge or add the magnitude of a negative charge.

Use this idea with the particle counts, charge and shell comparisons in this chapter. Next, different ions with the same electron count, isoelectronic ions, set up the radius comparisons of one point one point seven.
Protons equals Z, neutrons equals ay minus Z. Electrons equals Z in an atom, then adjust for the ion charge.
Why does a one minus ion have one more electron than its atom?

An ion has Z equals seventeen, ay equals thirty seven and charge minus one. Which counts are correct? seventeen protons, twenty neutrons, eighteen electrons seventeen protons, thirty seven neutrons, sixteen electrons twenty protons, seventeen neutrons, eighteen electrons seventeen protons, twenty neutrons, sixteen electrons ay Protons equals seventeen, neutrons equals thirty seven minus seventeen equals twenty, one extra electron gives eighteen electrons.
Shell number and nuclear attraction explain radius changes.

Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases as nuclear charge rises with similar shielding. Down a group, radius increases as extra shells add distance and shielding. Cations are smaller than their atoms, anions are larger. For isoelectronic ions, more protons means smaller radius.

Use this idea with the particle counts, charge and shell comparisons in this chapter. Ranking isoelectronic ions is the same same shell, more nuclear charge argument as across a period. The same attraction and shielding explain Ionisation energy.
Across a period radius falls, down a group it rises. Cations shrink, anions expand, more protons shrink isoelectronic ions.
Why does radius increase down a group despite increasing proton number?

What generally happens to atomic radius across a period? It decreases as greater nuclear charge pulls the same shell closer It increases because every element adds a new shell It stays constant because shielding rises greatly It increases because the nucleus is larger ay Proton number rises while electrons enter the same shell with similar shielding, so radius decreases.
Which statement about the structure of an atom is correct?
The nucleus is a very small, dense region holding the protons and neutrons, the electrons are in shells in the empty space around it.
Think about what sits at the centre of the atom and what sits around it.
Only two of the three types of subatomic particle are in the centre.
The electrons are outside the centre, in shells.
Describe the structure of an atom, in terms of its nucleus and the positions of the protons, neutrons and electrons.
A tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons sits at the centre, with electrons in shells in the mostly empty space around it.
Start with the centre of the atom, then move outwards.
Name the particles in the centre and say what is special about its size and density.
Finish with where the electrons are and what lies between them and the centre.
Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
The nucleus contains the protons and neutrons, the electrons are found in shells outside it.
Two of the three particles are found in the nucleus.
The nucleus holds the particles that make up almost all of the atom's mass.
One of the three has a negligible mass and is not in the nucleus.
Which statement compares the size of the nucleus with the size of the whole atom?
The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom. The electrons are in shells at a large distance from it and nothing lies between them.
Compare the diameter of the nucleus with the diameter of the whole atom.
The electron shells are far from the nucleus.
What is found in the region between the nucleus and the shells?
Explain what is meant by the statement an atom is mostly empty space.
The nucleus is tiny and the electrons are in shells far from it, with no particles between them, so most of the volume of the atom is empty.
Compare the size of the nucleus with the size of the atom.
Say where the electrons are relative to the nucleus.
Say what fills the region between the nucleus and the electron shells.

An atom of lithium has three protons, four neutrons and three electrons. part a, State where the protons and neutrons are found. part b, State where the electrons are found. part c, Explain why almost all of the mass of the atom is in one region.
The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, each of relative mass one, while the electrons in shells outside have a negligible mass.
Part part c, is about comparing the relative masses of the particles.
Which of the three particles is much lighter than the other two?
Link where the heavy particles are found to where the mass of the atom is.
Which row gives the relative charge and the relative mass of a neutron?
A neutron has no charge and has almost the same mass as a proton, so its relative mass is one.
The name of the particle is a clue to its charge.
Compare the mass of a neutron with the mass of a proton.
A neutron is about as heavy as a proton.
Which statement about protons, neutrons and electrons is correct?
Protons and neutrons both have a relative mass of one, but the neutron is uncharged. The electron is much lighter and has a relative charge of minus one.
List the relative mass and relative charge of each particle first.
One particle is far lighter than the other two.
Check each statement against your list, one at a time.
State the relative charge and the relative mass of an electron.
An electron has a relative charge of minus one and a relative mass of about one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six, which is negligible.
Give one value for charge and one value for mass.
The charge is the opposite of a proton's.
The mass is a very small fraction of the mass of a proton.
The relative mass of an electron is one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six, compared with one for a proton. Approximately how many electrons have the same total mass as one proton?

One proton has a relative mass of one and each electron has one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six, so the number of electrons is one divided by one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six.
The relative mass of an electron is a fraction of the mass of a proton.
To find how many small masses make up one large mass, divide the large by the small.
Divide one by the relative mass of one electron.
Which row is correct for an electron?
The electron carries the smallest negative charge, minus one, and has a relative mass of about one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six.
The sign of an electron's charge is opposite to a proton's.
The mass of an electron is much less than the mass of a proton.
Combine both facts, a negative charge and a very small mass.

A helium ion has two protons, two neutrons and one electron. part a, Calculate the overall relative charge of the ion. part b, Calculate the total relative mass of the protons and neutrons. part c, Explain why the electron can be ignored when giving the relative mass of the ion.
Two protons, plus two, and one electron, minus one, give plus one, the four protons and neutrons give a mass of four, and one electron adds only one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six.
Add up the charges of every particle, using the sign of each.
Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of one.
Compare the mass of an electron with the total mass of the other particles.
Define the term proton number, atomic number.
The proton number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which identifies the element.
The name of the quantity tells you what it counts.
Say which particle is counted and where it is found.
Mention the nucleus of an atom.
Define the term nucleon number, mass number.
The nucleon number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
A nucleon is a particle found in the nucleus.
Two types of particle are counted, not one.
Give a total of both types in the nucleus of an atom.
Which quantity is always the same for every atom of a particular element?
The proton number defines the element. Atoms of one element can have different numbers of neutrons, so different nucleon numbers.
Think about which number decides which element an atom belongs to.
Atoms of one element can differ in how many neutrons they have.
It is a count of particles in the nucleus that never changes for one element.

argon forty, forty kelvin and calcium forty are atoms of three different elements with proton numbers eighteen, nineteen and twenty. part a, State what these three atoms have in common. part b, Give the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in each atom.
All three have a nucleon number of forty. Protons equal the proton number, neutrons are forty minus that, and each neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.
The number forty written on each symbol is a clue to what they share.
Neutrons are found by subtracting the proton number from the nucleon number.
Each atom is neutral, so electrons equal protons.
Which statement describes the distribution of mass and charge in an atom?
The nucleus holds the protons, positive, and neutrons, so it has nearly all the mass and all the positive charge, the electrons carry the negative charge.
Which particles are in the nucleus, and which of them are charged?
The electrons have a negligible mass.
Put the heavy particles and the positive particles in the same place.
Describe the distribution of mass and charge within an atom.
Almost all the mass and all the positive charge are in the nucleus, and the negative electrons are in shells around it, an atom is neutral overall.
Treat mass and charge separately.
Say which region holds the positive charge and which holds the negative charge.
Finish with the overall charge of an atom.

A hydrogen one atom has a nucleus of one proton, relative mass one, and one electron, relative mass one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six. Calculate the percentage of the mass of the atom that is in the nucleus. Give your answer to four significant figures.
The total relative mass is one plus one over one thousand eight hundred and thirty six, so the nucleus contributes one divided by that total, expressed as a percentage.
Find the total relative mass of the atom first.
The fraction in the nucleus is the nucleus's mass divided by the total.
Convert the fraction to a percentage and check that it is just under the maximum possible.
Why does an atom have no overall electric charge?
Each proton has a charge of plus one and each electron minus one, so equal numbers give a total charge of zero. Neutrons carry no charge.
Think about which particles carry charge.
The charges of the two charged particles are equal in size and opposite in sign.
What must be true about their numbers for the charges to cancel?
The nucleus of an atom of element Y has a relative charge of plus nine and contains ten neutrons. Which row is correct for the atom?
A charge of plus nine means nine protons, so the neutral atom has nine electrons. The nucleus has nine protons and ten neutrons, so its relative mass is nineteen.
The charge of the nucleus tells you how many protons there are.
The atom is neutral, so its electrons balance the protons.
The relative mass of the nucleus counts both types of particle in it.
A student says, Most of the volume of an atom is the nucleus, and most of its mass is in the electrons. Explain why both parts of this statement are wrong.
The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom, and the protons and neutrons in it carry almost all the mass because electrons are so light.
Take the two claims one at a time, volume, then mass.
Compare the size of the nucleus with the region the electrons occupy.
Compare the relative mass of an electron with that of a proton or neutron.
Beams of protons, neutrons and electrons, all travelling at the same velocity, pass between a positive plate and a negative plate. Which row describes their behaviour?

Protons are positive so they move towards the negative plate, electrons are negative and move the other way. An electron has the same size of charge but far less mass, so it is deflected more, and neutrons are uncharged so go straight.
Decide the direction for each charged particle from its sign, then decide the size of the deflection.
Deflection depends on both the size of the charge and the mass.
Compare how heavy an electron is with a proton when the charges are equal in size.
Describe the behaviour of beams of protons, neutrons and electrons, all moving at the same velocity, in an electric field between a positive and a negative plate.
Protons go towards the negative plate, electrons towards the positive plate by a larger amount, and neutrons are not deflected.
Go through the three particles one at a time.
Neutrons have no charge, protons and electrons have opposite charges.
Finish by comparing the amount of deflection of the two charged beams.
The particles below all travel at the same velocity through the same electric field. Which is deflected by the smallest amount?
Deflection depends on charge divided by mass. The ratios are one, one half, two quarters equals one half and one quarter, so the smallest is for the ion with a single positive charge and mass four.
Work out charge divided by relative mass for each particle.
Two of the options have the same relative mass, so compare their charges.
The smallest charge to mass ratio gives the smallest deflection.
Explain why, at the same velocity, an electron is deflected much more than a proton in the same electric field, and in the opposite direction.
The opposite charge reverses the direction, the same sized charge on a far smaller mass gives a much larger charge to mass ratio.
Two things differ between an electron and a proton, the sign of the charge and the mass.
The sign decides the direction, the mass affects the size of the deflection.
Combine charge and mass into one ratio.
Calculate the total number of electrons in one carbonate ion, C O three two minus. The proton numbers are C equals six and O equals eight.
Neutral atoms give six plus three x eight electrons, and the two charge means two extra electrons.
Count the electrons in each atom in the formula first.
Remember that there are three oxygen atoms.
A negative charge means electrons have been added.
Which species has the same number of electrons as an atom of argon, proton number eighteen?
Argon has eighteen electrons. chloride has seventeen plus one equals eighteen electrons, while sulfur two plus has sixteen minus two equals fourteen, K has nineteen and sodium has eleven.
Work out the number of electrons in each species, one at a time.
A positive charge means electrons were lost, a negative charge means electrons were gained.
Start from the proton number of each element.

Give the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in each of these species. part a, aluminium twenty seven three plus, atomic number thirteen part b, bromine seventy nine minus, atomic number thirty five part c, sulfur thirty two two minus, atomic number sixteen part d, iron fifty six three plus, atomic number twenty six.
Protons are the bottom number, neutrons are top minus bottom, and electrons are protons minus the charge.
Read the two numbers on the left of each symbol before looking at the charge.
The neutrons never depend on the charge.
The charge changes only the number of electrons.
Which statement about atomic radius across Period three, from sodium to chlorine, is correct?
Across the period the electrons enter the same shell, so shielding is similar while the nuclear charge rises, the outer electrons are pulled closer.
Think about what changes across the period and what stays the same.
The number of shells is the same but the number of protons is not.
A stronger pull from the nucleus on the outer electrons has what effect on the radius?
Explain why the atomic radius decreases from sodium to chlorine across Period three.
More protons pull on outer electrons in the same shell with similar shielding, so the electrons are drawn in.
Say what changes in the nucleus, then what stays the same in the electron shells.
Compare the shell that is being filled for each element across the period.
Finish with the effect on the attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons.
Explain why atomic radius increases down Group two from beryllium to barium.
Each element down the group has an extra shell, so the outer electrons are further away and more shielded from the nuclear charge.
Compare the number of shells in beryllium and in barium.
Think about the distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus.
The extra protons are not enough to cancel the effect of the extra shells, say why.
Explain why the ionic radius of sodium plus is smaller than the atomic radius of sodium.
The atom loses its whole outer shell to form the ion, and the same eleven protons then pull the remaining electrons closer.
Compare the number of shells of electrons in the atom and in the ion.
The number of protons is unchanged when the ion forms.
Link the loss of the outer shell to the attraction from the nucleus.
Both sulfide and potassium plus contain eighteen electrons. Explain why the radius of the sulfide ion is larger than the radius of the potassium plus ion.
With the same electron arrangement, the ion with nineteen protons pulls the electrons in more strongly than the ion with sixteen.
Count the protons in each ion and compare the number of electrons.
The electron arrangements are identical.
The difference is in how strongly the nucleus attracts these electrons.
Which ion has the largest radius?
All four ions have ten electrons, so the one with the fewest protons, nine in fluoride, has the weakest pull on them and the largest radius.
Count the electrons in each ion.
When the electron arrangements are the same, compare the number of protons.
The ion with the least nuclear charge holds its electrons least tightly.
Which row shows the ions magnesium two plus, aluminium three plus, sodium plus and oxide in order of increasing radius?
All four have ten electrons, so the radius falls as the number of protons rises, aluminium three plus, thirteen, is smallest and oxide, eight, is largest.
Count the electrons in every ion before comparing them.
Rank them by proton number, not by the size of the charge.
More protons means a smaller ion when the electrons are the same.

The atomic radius of sodium is zero point one eight six nanometres and that of chlorine is zero point zero nine nine nanometres. part a, Explain why chlorine has a smaller atomic radius than sodium. part b, Explain why a sodium ion is smaller than a sodium atom. part c, Explain why a chloride ion is larger than a chlorine atom.
Part part a, is about nuclear charge in one shell, part b, is about losing a shell, and part c, is about extra electron repulsion with unchanged protons.
Each part uses a different idea, nuclear charge, shells, electron repulsion.
In part part b, compare the number of shells, in part part c, compare the number of electrons with the number of protons.
Say what changes and what stays the same for each pair.
Element X has six more protons than element Y. Which statement must be correct?

The smallest possible values are Y equals one and X equals seven, so X always has at least seven electrons and its first shell, two electrons, must be full. Option ay is the common wrong choice, more protons does not mean a larger atom, because radius decreases across a period, for example sodium to chlorine.
Try a few pairs of elements whose proton numbers differ by six.
Test each statement with a counter example before accepting it.
What is the smallest possible number of electrons in X?
Which row describes the relative sizes of the ionic radii of sodium plus, magnesium two plus and sulfide, from smallest to largest?

sodium plus and magnesium two plus both have ten electrons, and magnesium two plus has more protons so it is smaller. sulfide has eighteen electrons in three shells, so it is the largest. Option A wrongly ranks the ions by increasing proton number.
Count the electrons and shells in each ion.
Two of the ions have the same electron arrangement, compare their proton numbers.
The ion with an extra shell is biggest.
Technetium, Tc, is a second row transition element that does not occur naturally on Earth. One of its isotopes has fifty six neutrons. What is the nucleon number of this isotope?

Technetium has proton number forty three, so the nucleon number is forty three plus fifty six equals ninety nine. The other options give only the proton number, forty three, only the neutrons, fifty six, or twice the neutrons, one hundred and twelve.
Look up the proton number of technetium in the Periodic Table.
The nucleon number counts more than one type of particle.
Add the neutrons to the protons.
How many neutrons are contained in an atom of iron with a mass number of sixty?
Iron has proton number twenty six, so the neutrons are sixty minus twenty six equals thirty four. Option ay is the proton number and option D is the mass number.
Find the proton number of iron in the Periodic Table.
The mass number counts protons and neutrons together.
Subtract the protons from the mass number.

A helium ion contains two protons, two neutrons and one electron. This helium ion and a proton are passed separately through a uniform electric field, travelling at the same velocity. Which arrow describes the path of each particle? The positive plate is on the left and the negative plate on the right, arrows one and two bend towards the positive plate, three is undeflected, and four and five bend towards the negative plate, with five bending more than four.

Both particles are positive so both bend towards the negative plate. The proton has the greater charge to mass ratio, one against one quarter for the helium ion, so the proton is deflected more, five, and the helium ion less, four. Option D reverses this by ignoring the extra mass.
Decide which plate positive particles move towards.
Compare the charge to mass ratio of the two particles.
The particle with the larger ratio is deflected more.
What is the total number of protons, neutrons and electrons present in an ammonium ion with a relative formula mass of twenty one?

N H four plus has seven plus four equals eleven protons. It is a positive ion, so it has one fewer electron, ten. The neutrons make up the rest of the mass of twenty one, twenty one minus eleven equals ten. Option D forgets to remove an electron.
Add up the protons of all the atoms in the formula.
A positive ion has lost an electron.
Neutrons equals total mass minus the number of protons.
Which statement about iodine one three one, atomic number fifty three is correct?

Neutrons equals one hundred and thirty one minus fifty three equals seventy eight. A negative ion has gained an electron, so it has fifty three plus one equals fifty four electrons. Options ay and C subtract an electron for a negative ion, and ay and B give fifty three as the neutrons.
Find the neutrons from the two numbers on the symbol.
A negative ion has more electrons than protons.
Check that both the neutron number and the electron number in the option agree with your working.

Sodium azide, N ay N three, is an explosive used to inflate airbags in cars when they crash. It consists of positive sodium ions and negative azide ions. What are the numbers of electrons in the sodium ion and the azide ion?

sodium plus has eleven minus one equals ten electrons. The azide ion is nitrogen three minus, with three x seven equals twenty one electrons in the atoms plus one gained, twenty two. Options ay, C and D come from applying the charge in the wrong direction.
Find the electrons in the neutral atoms first, using the proton numbers.
Sodium ions are positive, electrons have been lost.
The azide ion is negative, electrons have been gained.
Which species contains a different number of electrons from the other three?

C L O four minus has seventeen plus thirty two plus one equals fifty electrons, H two S O four has two plus sixteen plus thirty two equals fifty, S O four two has sixteen plus thirty two plus two equals fifty, but tellurium two minus has fifty two plus two equals fifty four.
Add up the electrons of every atom in the formula using proton numbers.
Then add the electrons gained by a negative ion.
Three of the four species should give the same total.

The atomic radii and ionic radii for three elements in Period three are shown, element X has an atomic radius of zero point one one eight nanometres and an ionic radius of zero point zero five three nanometres, element Y has zero point zero nine nine nanometres and zero point one eight zero nanometres, element Z has zero point one six zero nanometres and zero point zero seven two nanometres. Using this data, which statement is correct?

The ionic radius of Y is larger than its atom, so Y forms an anion, a non metal, Z and X have ions smaller than their atoms, so they form cations, metals. A metal and a non metal form an ionic compound. Option D is wrong because Z loses electrons, and ay and B fail because X, a metal, conducts better and melts higher than the non metal Y.
Decide which elements form cations and which form an anion from the size change.
Use the ion sizes to decide which are metals.
Consider which two elements would have opposite charges.
In which row do the particles increase in size, from smallest to largest?

sodium plus, neon and fluoride all have ten electrons, and the number of protons falls, eleven, ten, nine, so the size increases. Options ay, B and C each show a series that decreases in size, because more protons pull the same electrons in more.
Count the electrons in each particle in every row.
Where the electron arrangements are identical, compare the number of protons.
Check whether each row goes up or down in size.
Why is the ionic radius of a sulfide ion larger than the ionic radius of a potassium ion?

Both ions have eighteen electrons in the same shells, so the ion with nineteen protons pulls them in more than the ion with sixteen. Options ay, B and D talk about trends or charge, but neither charge nor atomic number alone decides the size.
Count the electrons in each ion.
Compare the numbers of protons in the two nuclei.
When the electrons are the same, the nuclear charge decides the size.
An atom of calcium forty eight can form a two plus ion. Which statements about this ion are correct? one. It has twenty protons. two. It has twenty eight neutrons. three. It has twenty two electrons.

Which statements about an atom of technetium ninety nine are correct? one. It has thirteen fewer protons than neutrons. two. It forms ninety nine T c to the power of two plus which has forty five electrons. three. It has fifty six nucleons.
Sodium and sulfur react together to form sodium sulfide, N A two S. How do the atomic radius and ionic radius of sodium compare with those of sulfur? atomic radius ionic radius.

Which deductions about the. bismuth. two hundred and nine. eighty three atom are correct? one. It has eighty three electrons. two. It has one hundred and twenty six nucleons. three. It has eighty three neutrons.

A particular atom of germanium, germanium, has a nucleon number of seventy. Which statements about a. germanium. seventy. thirty two atom are correct? one. It has the same number of electrons as a. plus. two. seventy nine. thirty four S e ion. two. It has the same number of neutrons as an atom of sixty eight. thirty Z n. three. It has half as many protons as an atom of one hundred and sixty. sixty four G d.

A particular atom of germanium, germanium, has a nucleon number of seventy. Which statements about a. germanium. seventy. thirty two atom are correct? one. It has the same number of electrons as a. plus. two. seventy nine. thirty four S e ion. two. It has the same number of neutrons as an atom of sixty eight. thirty Z n. three. It has half as many protons as an atom of one hundred and sixty. sixty four G d.

Sodium and fluorine are both reactive elements. Two atoms are described. F. sodium atomic number. nine. eleven nucleon number. nineteen. twenty three. Which statements about these two atoms, and the ions they can form, are correct? one. One sodium atom has two more protons than one fluoride ion. two. One sodium atom has two more neutrons than one F atom. three. One sodium plus ion has the same number of electrons as one fluoride ion.
Which particle has equal numbers of protons and neutrons and an electronic structure of. one s squared two s squared two p to the sixth three s squared three p to the sixth?

The symbol for a phosphorus ion is. minus. three. thirty three. fifteen P. The symbol for a potassium ion is. plus. K. thirty seven. nineteen. What do these two ions have in common? one the same number of electrons. two the same number of neutrons. three the same number of protons.
In which ions are the number of electrons equal to the number of neutrons? one. minus. F. nineteen. nine. two. fifteen phosphide. three. plus. sodium. twenty three. eleven.
Which atom has the same number of electrons as an ammonium ion?
Which atom has the same number of electrons as the hydroxide ion, O H minus?
Which graph correctly shows relative electronegativity plotted against relative atomic radius for the elements sodium, magnesium, aluminium and silicon? electronegativity atomic radius.
Which element has the second smallest atomic radius in its group and the second highest electrical conductivity in its period?
Which ion has the smallest radius?
Which row describes the relative sizes of the ionic radii of sodium plus, magnesium two plus and sulfide? smallest largest.
In which species are the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons all different?

Three statements about potassium and chlorine and their ions are listed. The atomic radius of a potassium atom is greater than the atomic radius of a chlorine atom. one. The first ionisation energy of potassium is greater than the first ionisation energy of chlorine. two. The ionic radius of a potassium ion is greater than the ionic radius of a chloride ion. Which statements are correct? two and three.

Which row about silicon, silicon, and magnesium, magnesium, and their ions is correct? explanation comparison of silicon and magnesium. silicon has electrons in three p orbitals. magnesium has electrons in the three s orbital only. silicon has a greater atomic radius than magnesium.
Which particle contains eight protons, nine neutrons and ten electrons?

Sodium azide, N ay N three is an explosive used to inflate airbags in cars when they crash. It consists of positive sodium ions and negative azide ions. What are the numbers of electrons in the sodium ion and the azide ion? azide ion sodium ion. twenty. ten.

Which row about silicon, silicon, and magnesium, magnesium, and their ions is correct? explanation comparison of silicon and magnesium. silicon has electrons in three p orbitals. magnesium has electrons in the three s orbital only. silicon has a greater atomic radius than magnesium.

X and Y are elements in Period three of the Periodic Table. Y has a greater atomic number than X. The stable ion formed by Y has a greater radius than the stable ion formed by X. Sodium and sulfur react together to form sodium sulfide, N A two S. How do the atomic radius and ionic radius of sodium compare with those of sulfur? atomic radius ionic radius.

one point one Particles in the atom and atomic radius.
In one breath.

An atom is a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electron shells in mostly empty space, so almost all the mass sits in the nucleus. Counting the particles in atoms and ions, and comparing sizes across a period, down a group and between ions, all come from proton number, nucleon number and electron shells.
Key ideas.
Structure. Atoms are mostly empty space around a very small, dense nucleus that contains protons and neutrons. Electrons are found in shells in the empty space around the nucleus.

Distribution. Nearly all the mass and all the positive charge are in the nucleus, the negative charge is in the electron shells, and an atom is neutral because protons and electrons are equal in number.
Proton number, atomic number, Z is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. Nucleon number, mass number, ay is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

Electric field. Beams of protons, neutrons and electrons at the same velocity behave differently, protons are deflected towards the negative plate, electrons towards the positive plate by a larger angle, and neutrons are not deflected. Deflection depends on charge divided by mass.

Radius trends. Across a period the atomic radius decreases, nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell with similar shielding. Down a group it increases, extra shells put the outer electrons further away and more shielded. A cation is smaller than its atom, a shell is lost, an anion is larger than its atom, more electron repulsion, same nuclear charge. For ions with the same number of electrons, more protons means a smaller ion.

Ionic radius across a period. Compare ions with the same electron arrangement first, magnesium two plus is smaller than sodium plus because both have ten electrons in two shells, but magnesium has more protons. The stable Period three anions phosphorus three minus and sulfide each have eighteen electrons in three shells, within this pair, the greater nuclear charge makes sulfide smaller. Moving from Period three cations to anions therefore gives a sharp increase in ionic radius because the anions have an additional occupied shell, so there is no single steady decrease across the whole period. Down a group, comparable ions grow larger as another occupied shell is added, for example, bromide is larger than chloride despite bromine's greater nuclear charge.
Method.
Counting particles in an atom or ion.
Protons equals Z, the bottom number.
Neutrons equals ay minus Z.
Electrons in an atom equals Z. In an ion, electrons equals Z minus charge, so add the size of a negative charge and subtract a positive one.
For a compound ion add the electrons of every atom in the formula, then apply the charge.
Comparing sizes.
Count electrons and shells for each particle.
Same shells, more protons gives a smaller radius.
More shells, or more electrons with the same protons, gives a larger radius.

Traps.
Trap, More protons means a bigger atom. Why it's wrong, across a period the extra protons pull the electrons in more strongly and the radius falls. Instead, ask whether a new shell has been started.

Trap, A bigger ion charge means a bigger ion. Why it's wrong, magnesium two plus is smaller than sodium plus, the number of protons and electrons decides the size. Instead, count electrons, then compare protons.

Trap, Applying the charge the wrong way round, so chloride gets sixteen electrons. Why it's wrong, a negative ion has gained electrons. Instead, electrons equals Z minus charge with the sign included.

Trap, Heavier particles are deflected more. Why it's wrong, deflection depends on charge divided by mass, so an electron is deflected far more than a proton. Instead, work out the charge to mass ratio.
Trap, The nucleus fills most of the atom. Why it's wrong, it is tiny, the atom is mostly empty space. Instead, say it is small but holds nearly all the mass.
